As we go through, ladies and gentlemen, I'll be repeating quite a lot of things in terms of the terminology. It's not because I think you're daft, it's because I'm well aware from personal experience that a lot of the terminology in this case are things that people who are not medics just don't know. Sometimes a bit of repetition helps to reinforce some of the important points, so when you get to hear the evidence about the children, you already have a reasonable working knowledge of what people are talking about.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: The witnesses will explain as we go along, but sometimes repetition of the important terms at an early stage can help us all, not least me.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So if we can just open the glossary at page 2 because there's something I'm going to come to in a second, just while you've got it there. I'll direct you to it in a minute. But I'm going to move on now to the third child, who is [Baby C].
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: The charge, the count, relating to [Baby C] is count 3 and the allegation is that Lucy Letby murdered [Baby C] on 14 June 2015.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: [Baby C] was born on 10 June 2015. He, like so many other of the children in this case, was premature. His gestational age was 30 weeks and 1 day. You'll remember, I told you yesterday, 40 weeks is the standard, if there is such a thing, length of pregnancy.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Anything 37 weeks plus is regarded by the medics as a full term baby. So significantly premature at 30 weeks and a day.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: He was born to [Parents of Baby C], his parents, and [Baby C]'s growth in the womb had been restricted because of a problem with
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: the placenta. The placenta, you all know without me telling you, I'm sure, is sometimes referred to as the afterbirth.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: [Baby C] weighed 800 grams when he was born, so that's less than 2 pounds in imperial measurements. But despite that, he was born in good condition. He didn't require any resuscitation at birth and he had high Apgar scores.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: You can see on that second page that I have just asked you to keep open in the glossary that the Apgar test is a scoring system that evaluates the physical condition of the newborn child at 1 minute after birth, 5 minutes after birth and also 10 minutes after birth.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: You'll hear these scores being given in evidence in due course, but for present purposes all you need to know is that his scores were good. So premature, but in good condition.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: He, that is [Baby C], was admitted into nursery 1 of the neonatal unit. He began to show signs of breathing distress and so was intubated. Intubated means a tube was put down his throat to help him breathe. So put on to a ventilator to help him breathe.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: He was also given a drug or a substance which is called surfactant, and this is something that you will hear mentioned in many of these cases. If you go to page 22 of the glossary:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "Surfactant is a naturally occurring protein that helps to reduce surface tension in the lungs, thereby keeping the lungs open and closed [I think it should say]. It is missing in premature babies, therefore artificial surfactant is given to prevent babies developing stiff lungs."
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So putting it in more straightforward language, it's a protein that helps the lungs and therefore helps the baby to breathe.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: The following day after his birth, so 11 June, the tube was taken out -- the doctors would say he was extubated -- so "ex", as in out, "tube" -- and put on a form of breathing support called CPAP.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: He had a line, a catheter, in through his belly button, which was designed to give him fluids and medicines. That fell out at about 6 o'clock in the morning on 12 June -- so this is now day 3 for [Baby C] -- and that caused him a brief period of hypoglycaemia, low blood sugar. You'll find all these terms in the glossary, so hypo, low, glycaemia, low blood sugar.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Hyperglycaemia, high blood sugar.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So a long line, so another intravenous line, was fitted to [Baby C], and he was X-rayed, his abdomen was X-rayed, and the point of the X-ray was to check that the line was in the correct position. That X-ray showed that he had an abnormal build-up of gas in his abdomen and his stomach was swollen and the loops of his small bowel, remember the intestines that go almost like a winding river down through the abdomen from the stomach to the rectum, there was gas in the small bowel.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: That can be -- this is a theme that you'll hear being developed in the evidence -- a feature of the sort of breathing support that [Baby C] was on.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: The breathing support that [Baby C] was given was reduced and, having managed a period of independent breathing, so breathing without any support at all, he was placed on something called Optiflow, which is the least invasive form of breathing support. And that was by noon on 13 June. So day 1, when he was born, the 10th. Then 11th, 12th, 13th, so day 4 for [Baby C].
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: You'll remember me telling you yesterday that when nurses feed very small premature babies, they use the nasogastric tube, the tube that goes up the nose and down into the stomach. Before they feed, they'll draw it back, they'll suck the stomach contents out to see if there's any undigested food in the stomach. So for reasons that you'll hear explained in the evidence, very important. You'll hear me coming back and back and back to this point as I develop this explanation.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: When they did this, when they -- they call it aspiration -- so when they sucked out the stomach contents, the nurse found some bile, traces of bile. If there are traces of bile in the stomach, that can be an early sign of something called necrotising enterocolitis.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: If we just go to that in here in page 16 of the glossary, please. You'll see necrotising enterocolitis, often referred to as NEC, for obvious reasons, listening to me trying to say it, it's a serious gastrointestinal disorder where a portion of the bowel becomes inflamed and may die. It typically occurs in newborns that are either premature or otherwise unwell. Symptoms of NEC may include food intolerance, abdominal distension -- so swelling of the abdomen -- abdominal pain, blood in the stool, vomiting or bile aspirate, so what I have just said, bile being sucked up through the NEC (sic) before the feed. And it gives a number of other potential symptoms there.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Then the definition goes on to say it's:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "The most common gastrointestinal emergency occurring in neonates and affected infants will not tolerate their feeds or
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: have progressive symptoms including aspirates [milk from the stomach after a feed because it's not been digested], abdominal distension... pain... and other evidence of (inaudible: coughing)."
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Then at the end:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "It's a serious gastrointestinal emergency."
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So any signs of NEC are taken very seriously.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: [Baby C] was given treatment for that potential problem -- I say potential problem because it hadn't been confirmed -- and part of that treatment was to stop his feeds. Obviously, you don't want to be putting more food into an infant that's got a bowel problem for reasons that are probably so obvious they don't need me to explain them.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: But by the evening of the same day, so we've gone from noon to the evening, [Baby C] was fine and the decision was taken to start milk feeds again and he was doing well.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: The night shift of the 13th into the 14th, so 8 pm to 8 am, you will remember, is one of the few shifts in this case that we don't have records of which child was in which of the four nurseries. So this is -- there's a gap in the records for this particular shift.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: A nurse called Sophie Ellis was allocated responsibility for caring for [Baby C] in room number 1, so she was the designated nurse. And Sophie Ellis was less qualified than Lucy Letby. Do you remember me telling you about the hierarchical structure yesterday?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Number 6 at the top, 4 in the middle, and the sub-division of 5s, the 5 with the ICU training, which Lucy Letby was one of those, and the 5s without that qualification.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: But Sophie Ellis, albeit she wasn't as well qualified as Lucy Letby, was given the care of [Baby C] because he was stable. So it's not simply a question of looking at where a child is in terms of which room they're in, but there is an assessment by the medical staff of whether a child is stable or unstable. Again, this is something we'll come back to as we go through the explanation.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Lucy Letby was the designated nurse for another child and I'll use this child's initials for the reasons I told you yesterday. We'll call him JE. JE was in room 3. So if you were to look at this simplistically, you'd say [Baby C] in room 1 is in a worse condition than JE, who's in room 3. But as a matter of fact, on
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: this occasion, that wasn't the view of the medical staff. Because although JE was in room number 3, [Nurse B], who was the shift leader, who was the senior nurse on duty, had assigned him to Lucy Letby because, in [Nurse B]'s opinion, [Baby C] was of more concern and he appeared to be deteriorating at the start of the shift.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Did I say [Baby C]? I meant JE was deteriorating, sorry. So JE in room number 3. Lucy Letby looking after/designated to JE. He is deteriorating and the sign of deterioration in his case was that he was grunting. In this context, grunting means that there are breathing difficulties. Okay? With these very small babies, if they make grunting sounds, that's a red flag for potential breathing problems.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So Lucy Letby was told that she needed to keep a really close eye on him because that was not normal behaviour for JE. That was a message that [Nurse B] had to reinforce later in the shift when it became apparent to [Nurse B] that Lucy Letby was ignoring what she'd been told.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: [Baby C], on the other hand, was first fed milk that night at 23.00 hours, so 11 o'clock on 13 June. He was being given really tiny quantities. Sophie Ellis put half a millilitre of milk into his nasogastric tube, a tiny, tiny quantity. It goes into the tube and it passes down in a sort of syphon effect under the force of gravity -- the baby there, end of tube here, (indicating). It goes in and goes down under the force of gravity.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: And 15 minutes after Sophie Ellis had given [Baby C] this tiny quantity of milk, she checked that he was stable and she left nursery number 1 to go to the nurses' station, which is just outside the room.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: When she was there at the nurses' station, she heard the monitor alarm, the monitor that was connected to [Baby C]. She heard it alarm. And when she went back into nursery 1, there was Lucy Letby standing next to [Baby C]'s incubator. So Lucy Letby, who should have been in room number 3 and had been told off by [Nurse B] for not looking after JE who was grunting, had no business, we would say, with [Baby C], and yet when the alarm went off, there was Lucy Letby.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Lucy Letby said to Sophie Ellis, "He's just dropped his heart rate and saturations", so his heart rate had gone down, what the medics call bradycardia, so that's a low heart rate. Tachycardia, it's a phrase some people know probably, means a fast heart rate. So a brady or a bradycardia, low heart rate, "He's just dropped his heart rate and saturations."
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So here we have, ladies and gentlemen, the third baby who had suffered a serious deterioration in that neonatal unit in a matter of less than a week and there again, at the bedside or at the incubator side, was Lucy Letby.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Nurse Taylor remembers being called over by Sophie Ellis about half an hour later. [Baby C] was desaturating, his heart rate was dropping, and she used what's called a Neopuff device to try and help him with his breathing. I'm just going to show you part of a video, you'll see the full video in due course, but just to give you an idea of what I'm talking about by a Neopuff.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: (Video played to the court)
There is sound that goes with this, but I'm just going to play you the video for now so you can visualise what it is I'm talking about.

So the working end, so to speak, or the important end is that little cup in the nurse's hand that goes over the mouth of the child. This gives oxygen to the child to help with resuscitation. So it's a non-invasive form of resuscitation that's used by the nurses to keep a child who is in crisis going until the doctors arrive because it's the doctors that are qualified to put in the breathing tubes, put the tube down the throat, and hook up the child to a ventilator.

When the Neopuff was used, [Baby C] quickly recovered, but within a short time again he had prolonged desaturation, so his oxygen content in his blood was falling and his heart was slowing again, and this time a crash call was put out.

Ladies and gentlemen, you might get the impression from what you've heard from me since 2 o'clock yesterday afternoon that babies collapsing in this way was a common event in a neonatal unit because this was the third that I've told you about in a few days. But this was the first time Sophie Ellis had ever seen a collapse and resuscitation. So one of the nurses who was there, this was the first time she'd ever seen it. That's how uncommon these events were in that unit, and yet three in a matter of days.
As [Baby C] collapsed for what proved to be the final time, Lucy Letby said to Sophie Ellis, "He's going, he's going", and she was right.

Now, evidence that the police subsequently obtained from a mobile phone that had been seized from Lucy Letby gives us and you an insight into what Lucy Letby was actually doing immediately before [Baby C] collapsed, as does material from the
medical records of other children who were in the unit at the time.

You already know she was supposed, Lucy Letby was supposed, to be looking after JE in room number 3, but she didn't want that. Do you remember me telling you that [Nurse B] had told her off? Lucy Letby didn't want to be looking after JE in room number 3 because she texted an off-duty colleague saying that she, Lucy Letby, wanted to be in room number 1, because it would be cathartic for her. In other words, it would help her well-being, she was saying, to see a living baby in the space that had previously been occupied by a dead baby, [Baby A], the baby that had died a few days earlier under her care. But [Nurse B] had put her in room 3, so she didn't like it.

In the records of JE, Lucy Letby recorded herself as having checked in on him at 10 pm, 22.00 hours. One of the observations that she recorded in JE's notes was that he was grunting. Do you remember me telling you, that's a problem? You might expect that in all the circumstances, and particularly after the death of [Baby A] and the near fatal collapse of [Baby B] a few days earlier, that would have caused her some concern and that she would have stayed with this child, who was exhibiting breathing problems, JE. But she didn't.

Between 10 pm and 11 pm she's recorded as having checked the medication for other babies, three other babies. They were in another room. But the medicines were stored in room number 1, where [Baby C] was, and at 10.21, she co-signed with [Nurse B] in the notes of yet another child.
Although she had no specifically allocated responsibilities in room number 1, Lucy Letby texted her friend at 10.34, 22.34, and she said:
"I've done a couple of meds in 1 [ie room 1], I'll be fine."
At 10.53 she texted:
"Just a shame I was on with Mel and [Nurse B]. Sophie in 1 so I haven't got her to talk to either."
At 11 pm, she was back in room number 3 with JE, and she took some observations from another child at the same time, who I'll refer to as PE.
At 11.09 she sent a text referring to the image of [Baby A], the dead [Baby A], that she had in her head from the week before and then texted her friend, "Sleep well", followed by two kisses.
[Baby C]'s collapse was documented in the notes and timed 7 minutes later, at 23.15, just before she uttered the line, "He's going".

Now, when the crash call went out, the senior house officer and the registrar responded promptly. They used what is called, what I'll probably mispronounce as a Guedel airway to help [Baby C] breathe. The registrar was a Dr Katherine Davis. She made efforts to intubate, to put a tube down [Baby C]'s throat, but she didn't succeed, and the reason she didn't succeed was that [Baby C]'s vocal cords were swollen. When she looked -- the doctors look down the throat of the patient before they put the tube in. When she looked down she saw that [Baby C]'s vocal cords were swollen. This is another feature that we'll return to in other cases.

The consultant, Dr Gibbs, who was the senior, the most experienced consultant, attended. He successfully intubated [Baby C] and took over a prolonged effort to resuscitate him, but he did not succeed. Tragically, he did not succeed, and [Baby C] was pronounced dead after a long effort at resuscitation at 5.58 on the morning of 14 June 2015.
A post-mortem examination was conducted 2 days later. A Dr Kokai gave the cause of death as:
"Widespread hypoxic ischaemic damage to the heart/myocardium due to lung disease."
He gave some other contributing factors as well.

But the important thing here, ladies and gentlemen, is [Baby C] did not have NEC. In isolation, you'll be wondering why I'm emphasising that. As we go through, you'll understand why that becomes an important fact.

The independent medical experts who reviewed these cases gave their opinions. Dr Dewi Evans thought that infection was a significant factor in [Baby C]'s collapse but did not adequately explain it and he expressed concerns about the cause of [Baby C]'s sudden deterioration. He concluded that the swelling to the gastric area that I told you about could be the consequence of using the breathing support, but he also thought it could be suspicious in the context of all the other cases that you are going to hear about. And importantly, he was of the view that the damage to [Baby C]'s heart was the result of rather than the cause of his collapse. So he was looking at the pathologist at the time's findings about hypoxic ischaemic damage to the heart -- in simple terms, lack of oxygen damage -- and he said that wasn't what caused him to collapse, that was the result of the collapse.

Dr Bohin, Sandie Bohin's view was that although [Baby C] had pneumonia at the time of his death she believed that was not the cause of death. She agreed with Dr Evans that infection was a contributory factor in the sense that it made [Baby C] less responsive to resuscitation and she agreed with Dr Evans that the damage noted to [Baby C]'s heart had occurred after he had collapsed and therefore did not cause it.
She couldn't identify any pathological process or condition to account for the inflation of [Baby C]'s gastric area. She thought it was too gross to be the consequence of CPAP.

She both agreed and disagreed with Dr Evans over the cause of that abdominal gas and thought that it could be a case of someone having deliberately inserted air into the nasogastric tube, into the stomach, but that wasn't the only possibility. And because Dr Bohin thought that this was very concerning and had no clear cause, she conducted a full review of the notes to determine whether or not the NGT, the tube, the nasogastric tube, had been on free drainage, what they call free drainage, at the time of or before the swelling that had been noted on 12 June.

Free drainage, in a very short explanation, and you'll get the proper explanation from the witnesses, not from me, but free drainage means almost what it says: if there's air in there, if the tube is on free drainage, if it's uncapped, the air can escape back through the tube. Okay? And if a tube's on free drainage, it means that if you get a build-up of air in the stomach then, rather than having to go through the intestines and out of the bottom end, it can come out through the tube.

Dr Bohin's close examination of the notes found a nursing record on 13 June, so the day before [Baby C]'s death, showing that the tube had been on free drainage and, more importantly, the nurses were aspirating the tube every 3 or 4 hours. In other words, they were deliberately pulling out the stomach contents every 3 or 4 hours up the tube to check that there was no excess gas or liquid. And when that was done every 3 or 4 hours, the aspiration, pulling up of the contents, yielded only small volumes, half of 1 millilitre.

So it follows from that, ladies and gentlemen, from the fact that this exercise was being undertaken every 3 or 4 hours, that any suggestion that the build-up of gas when [Baby C] collapsed had started with CPAP, with the breathing support, it doesn't work because if that was the cause, it would have been pulled out.

Therefore, a rather long run-up to the wicket, leads to the conclusion of Dr Bohin that the only feasible mechanism for the excessive air in [Baby C]'s gastrointestinal system, his stomach and his bowel, the only feasible explanation or mechanism for that at the time of his collapse was because someone had deliberately put air into [Baby C] down the nasogastric tube. In other words, [Baby C] was killed by air injected into his stomach through the nasogastric tube. So this isn't a case of injecting air into the bloodstream, this is a case of air going in through the NGT.
So it was a variation or a refinement of a theme that Lucy Letby had started with the [Babies A & B] twins.
We will see, as we go through the balance of the 17 cases, this method being replicated on other children.

A radiologist, a doctor with expertise in interpreting X-rays and scans, Dr Owen Arthurs, looked at the scans of [Baby C] and he thought that what you could see was consistent with, not necessarily diagnostic of but consistent with, air being inserted into [Baby C] in this way down the nasogastric tube.

Dr Marnerides, who is the independent pathologist, concluded that the ischaemic changes to [Baby C]'s heart -- and "ischaemic" means changes caused by a lack of blood flow and a lack of oxygen -- were most likely caused by the prolonged unsuccessful resuscitation. So in other words, he agreed with Dr Bohin and Dr Evans that the heart problem was the result of the resuscitation; it's not the cause of the need for resuscitation. So the collapse was nothing to do with the heart problem.

He noted that the microscopic histological examination of the lungs confirmed that [Baby C] had pneumonia, but he concluded from all the findings that [Baby C] had died as a result of having an excessive quantity of air injected into his stomach, down the nasogastric tube, the NGT.
The effect of that, ladies and gentlemen, I don't know if you can visualise now -- in fact, if we can put it on the screen, please. It's the NGT video, please.
(Video played to the court)
This is subject to the expert evidence, okay, ladies and gentlemen? So health warning: a barrister telling you about the human body is not a reliable source. Okay?
You can see the stomach in green and you can see directly above the stomach, the heart. Thank you. Then to either side of the heart you can see the lungs.

Between the lungs and the stomach is a sort of slightly crescentic muscle, which is the diaphragm, so it's under the heart -- that's it, so across there (indicating), running the full width almost of the body. Can you see what I'm talking about? It sort of goes like that (indicating) under the heart.

If you inflate the stomach with air, it expands like a balloon and it puts pressure on the diaphragm and it splints, we'll call it, the diaphragm. And it's the diaphragm that -- it's the use of the diaphragm that enables you to breathe. If you splint the diaphragm, you either reduce or eliminate its effectiveness and it means you can't breathe. It's in effect putting pressure on the lungs. We'll get a proper explanation of this from the doctors, but that's the mechanism, if you like, of how inflating a baby's stomach with either air or milk or a combination of those two things will stop a baby breathing.

You can also put pressure on something called the vagus nerve, which also can slow the heart rate. It was that -- it was that inflation of the stomach that led to [Baby C]'s breathing being compromised and him then suffering a cardiac arrest. So if you're trying to murder a child in a neonatal unit, it's a fairly effective way of doing it. It doesn't really leave much of a trace.
The staff on duty in the unit at the time of [Baby C]'s collapse, or just after, were the consultant, Dr Gibbs -- I suppose he's a physician, not a surgeon.
So Dr Gibbs, registrar Dr Katherine Davis, senior house officer Jian Minh Hor, the nurses [Nurse B], Lucy Letby, Sophie Ellis, Melanie Taylor and Nicola Dennison.
And even if you can't remember the names, ladies and gentlemen, you'll remember what I showed you yesterday, the correlation between these events and who is on duty.

I think we're either -- I think Lucy Letby, by the third episode, is the only person who was present at this and the preceding two events. You can imagine how -- and you have seen in that table -- although she's there every time, the next highest number of times anyone else was there is much, much lower.

Lucy Letby was interviewed in July 2018. She confirmed that JE, the boy that she was looking after, had been in room 3. She denied that she'd had anything to do with [Baby C] other than during the resuscitation.

She said that she'd not been the person who discovered the problem with [Baby C], although we say her texts put her in the room. She associated [Baby C]'s problem with his first feed, the implication being that she believed that this was a case of NEC. And she couldn't remember how it was that she had ended up in room number 1.

In an interview a year later, she said again that JE had been in room 3, she'd been his nurse, and then she said that she might have been in room number 1 because she was getting drugs from the cupboard or checking the resuscitation trolley, which was kept in room number 1.

She was then asked about the text messages, which by then the police had recovered from her phone. She said that she might have been sending them from the nurses' station and then gone into room number 1 "to do something else".
She then agreed in this second interview in 2019 that she'd been the only person in the room when [Baby C] had collapsed.

On 14 June, back to 2015 now, ladies and gentlemen, at 15.52, Lucy Letby had searched on Facebook for [Baby C]'s parents. That was the first of her days off, having come off duty at about 8 o'clock that morning. The timing may well suggest that having just done a night shift, it was one of the first things she did when she woke up.

So again, ladies and gentlemen, it's important always, we suggest, to keep a sense of perspective in this case. It's very easy to get dragged in by the detail. But there was and there is a pattern emerging, we suggest. So far as the nursing staff were concerned, Lucy Letby was the only person that was working when [Baby C] collapsed who had also been working when [Baby A] and [Baby B] had died and collapsed.

She was the only person in the room when [Baby C] collapsed, just as she had been by the side of [Baby A] when he collapsed and had been one of two in the room when [Baby B] collapsed. Not only did she have no reason to be in the room when [Baby C] collapsed, but she should have been in room number 3, keeping an eye on JE, having already been told off for failing to do so.

As I said earlier, we'll come back to the issue of the swollen vocal cords in [Baby C] that were seen by the doctor, who was trying to -- was it Dr Davis -- who tried to intubate [Baby C] when he first collapsed.
What we're going to see as we progress, ladies and gentlemen, is that Lucy Letby's method of attacking these children in the NNU was beginning to develop. She had injected air into the

bloodstream of the [Babies A & B] twins. She'd varied that approach by injecting air down the nasogastric tube of [Baby C] and, as I said earlier, the method she used on [Baby C] was one she replicated in some of the later cases.
I'm going to move on now to [Baby D].
[Baby D] was born just less than a week after [Baby C] died. You will find reference to [Baby D] in count 4 on the indictment. This also is an allegation of murder. It's on page 2 of the indictment.

[Baby D] was a baby that would be classified as full term because she was born to [Parents of Baby D] at a gestational age of 37 weeks and 1 day. And she was delivered by C-section. The risk factor so far as [Baby D] was concerned, albeit she was full term, was that her mum [Mother of Baby C]'s waters had broken early and [Mother of Baby C] should have been given antibiotics to stave off infection, but she was not. That failure is a legitimate target of criticism in her care.

But despite that fact, [Baby D] was born in good condition. She had a normal birth weight, but 12 minutes after she had been born, she needed some help because she lost colour and became floppy in her father's arms. She was put under observation because of the issue with her mum's waters breaking early and she began to show signs of respiratory distress, grunting.
Do you remember JE in room 3? Exactly the same problem.
And [Baby D]'s temperature dropped.

Those two factors should have prompted an immediate medical review as those two signs together are indicative of infection, which is the sort of problem you would expect or you would anticipate at least when a mother's waters break far in advance of giving birth.

A review eventually took place when [Baby D] refused to feed and had poor colour. And because of these problems, [Baby D] was admitted into nursery number 1 at the neonatal unit and she was put into an incubator.
She was given supplemental oxygen through that Neopuff machine that I showed you earlier, and she was fed by fluids and given antibiotics to stave off infection.
She developed a very high temperature and also had a high heart rate. And because of that, she was -- a tube was put down her

throat, so she was intubated, and put on to a ventilator. In order to do that, the doctors essentially paralyse you so that you don't fight against the -- so that the child doesn't fight against the ventilator.

After that treatment was given, [Baby D] improved significantly, but was still affected by her infection, and although X-rays that were taken showed no obvious signs of infection, the clinical picture, what the doctors were seeing in the patient, in the sense of looking at the patient and how she was behaving, suggested that she had an infection. So that, ladies and gentlemen, was 20 June.

The following day, the 21st, [Baby D] was breathing for herself, so no tube, no supplemental oxygen, and what -- the doctors use a shorthand SVIA, self-ventilating in air. So doesn't need any extra oxygen, doesn't need any support in terms of a machine or anything like that.
So she managed that, which obviously is a good sign, she was then given a bit of extra support using the CPAP machine, but air -- so no extra oxygen, just the machine to help with the breathing.

Catheters were put into [Baby D]'s umbilical cord, so to get access, get a line in through the umbilical cord into [Baby D]'s vein system and her arterial system, so blood coming out and blood going back to the heart. And the test for infection showed a decrease in the markers for infection, signs of infection, to a low level, and other tests and observations were normal, and [Baby D] was started on feeds. So all good signs on 21 June.
The general picture was that although she was ill, [Baby D] was responding well to treatment and was not expected to deteriorate.

During the night shift of the 21st into the 22nd June, which was a Sunday, nurse Caroline Oakley was given -- was made the designated nurse for [Baby D], who was one of three children in room number 1.
Nurse Oakley also had a child for whom she was the designated nurse in room number 2, a child who I'll refer to by the initials GC.

[Baby D] in room number 1, GC in room number 2, Caroline Oakley designated nurse for both. There were two other children in room number 1 with [Baby D]. The designated nurse for the other two was Lucy Letby. They were JE, who was the boy who had had the grunting issue when in room number 3 when [Baby C], we say, was murdered by Lucy Letby, and another child, ME. So JE and ME.

On that night shift, [Baby D] collapsed three separate times. The first at about 1.30 in the morning, the second at 3 o'clock, and finally at 3.45 on Monday, 22 June. On each occasion that [Baby D] collapsed, those who attended, the medics who attended, were struck by the sight of mottling and poor perfusion and brown/black discolouration to her skin, mainly over her trunk.
We've heard that sort of thing before, haven't we?
The prosecution say this was another case of injecting a child with air into the bloodstream. So intravenous -- into the venous system -- embolus.
Intravenous embolus, the same mode of attack that had been deployed with the [Babies A & B] twins.
Just coming back slightly, first collapse at 1.30.

At 1.15, 15 minutes before [Baby D]'s first collapse, Caroline Oakley checked [Baby D]. At 1.25, 5 minutes before [Baby D]'s first collapse, the notes say that Caroline Oakley and Lucy Letby started an infusion for [Baby D]. In other words, a liquid going in through a line into [Baby D]'s bloodstream.
Remember [Baby A]? There is also a note in the feeding chart of an aspirate at 1.30, so this drawing-up of liquid through the nasogastric tube.
So Lucy Letby hands-on with [Baby D] in the minutes before she collapsed through an air embolus, we say.

Dr Emily Thomas, who made a note of 1.29 had noted an unusual rash, what she noted in the notes as "a spreading, non-blanching rash". When that was first noticed, Caroline Oakley, who you will remember was the designated nurse, and was responsible with Lucy Letby for starting the infusion at 1.25, when that was noted, Caroline Oakley was away from [Baby D]. So the designated nurse, out of the room. Because there is a record in the notes that Caroline Oakley made, saying that she was called back by Lucy Letby, and a nurse with the surname Percival-Ward.

There's a suggestion that the shift leader, [Nurse C], noticed that [Baby D] was stiff and had an odd discolouration of the skin. There's a note made by Lucy Letby in JE's records, one of the other children in room number 1, that she was engaged with him at the time everyone else was responding to the emergency with [Baby D].
Well, if Lucy Letby's note is right, how could she have been the person that called back the designated nurse? Unless of course

what she wrote in somebody else's notes isn't true. We'll come back to that in the context of other cases. Unless she was setting herself up with an alibi in somebody else's notes: it couldn't have been me because at that time I was doing this with another patient.

We know what time the crash team arrived, the doctors arrived, because, as you would expect, you have to use a pass to get in and there is an electronic record. It's not an invariable record, it has to be said there are holes in the records, but we know on this occasion when the three doctors arrived because their security passes have registered on the system. And in that first episode, [Baby D] was successfully resuscitated. She settled back to normal with normal sats, normal saturations, the oxygen content of the blood, and normal blood gas results. But as I said, a further episode at 3 o'clock.

About 20 minutes before that, Lucy Letby and Caroline Oakley had administered some medication to [Baby D] and Caroline Oakley then updated the computer records for [Baby D] before going to another baby in room number 2, the baby ME. So Caroline Oakley again leaves the room. Lucy Letby, the designated nurse for the other two children in room number 1. So again immediately before the collapse, the second collapse of [Baby D] that night, the designated nurse leaves the room, leaving a single person in room. As always, we suggest Lucy Letby.

The medical team was called again when [Baby D] collapsed for the second time and they saw similar discolouration to what they'd seen the first time, the signs, we suggest, of the air embolus, the air into the bloodstream, although it was said it was less severe than it had been on the first occasion.

This time, [Baby D] was distressed and crying. As you will hear from the experts, that can be a sign consistent with air embolus. Once again, [Baby D] was resuscitated, but Lucy Letby didn't leave it there.

[Baby D]'s records show that at 3.20, Lucy Letby started another infusion for [Baby D]. We know that she remained in the room, if her records are accurate, because there's a record in JE's notes that she did something at 3.30 for him.

At 3.45, [Baby D]'s monitor alarmed again, and this was [Baby D]'s third and final collapse. When the medical staff arrived, when the doctors arrived, CPR was in progress, all resuscitative efforts were unsuccessful and, sadly, treatment was withdrawn at 4.21. [Baby D] was pronounced dead at 4.25 on 22 June. Her death was reported to the coroner and at the time the cause of death was given as pneumonia with acute lung injury.

So, ladies and gentlemen, in a two-week period, three children had died and one had had a life-threatening episode in the neonatal unit at the Countess of Chester Hospital, and Lucy Letby was the only constant presence.

These events and the records were again reviewed by independent experts. Dr Dewi Evans observed that [Baby D]'s clinical course, exhibiting a window of near recovery on two occasions followed by a third collapse, was not consistent with the fatal evolution of pneumonia.

If a child dies from pneumonia, ladies and gentlemen, where the symptoms are present at birth, the child tends to show a clinical course that's unrelenting and progressive, despite medical intervention. So in other words, a decline to death which isn't helped by doctors intervening. And that is patently obviously not the case with [Baby D]. And Dr Evans concluded that the discolouration, this fleeting rash observed by the treating medics was indicative of another case of air embolism.

Dr Sandie Bohin, the other independent paediatrician, noted that whilst there was clear evidence of infection, [Baby D] had improved after the first two interventions. In her view, in Dr Bohin's view, [Baby D]'s clinical status at 7 pm on 21 June was not that of a deteriorating baby who would be dead a few hours later.

Dr Bohin thought that this skin rash, this moving rash, was abnormal. She excluded the possibility of it being bruising because it disappeared and we all know, you don't have to be doctors, we all know that bruising doesn't just disappear. And she thought that findings or observations at the time, findings on X-rays after death, were all consistent with Dr Evans' view that this was a case of intravenous air embolus.

In case it's a question that's occurring to you, ladies and gentlemen, Dr Bohin's view was that injecting a child of this size with as little as 3 to 5 millilitres per kilo of air is sufficient to kill. It doesn't take much. And Dr Bohin refers to published medical texts about air embolus, in which on very, very rare occasions there are documented cases of accidental air embolus, but the subject of air embolus often exhibits signs of extreme terror, it's a physiological response. She thought that was consistent with what was being described about [Baby D].

Ladies and gentlemen, this isn't just looking at one case this isolation. We say you have to, and you should, look at what happened to [Baby D] in the context of what had gone before and what was to follow.
Dr Marnerides, the pathologist, phrased it this way: that [Baby D] died with pneumonia, not from pneumonia.
It's a bit like the heart issue with [Baby C].

He was of the view that this was a case of deliberate injection of air into what he refers to as a vascular access line. In other words, a line that gives access to the vascular system, to the bloodstream. That sort of thing just doesn't happen by mistake.

Dr Arthurs, the radiologist who looked at the scans or the Xrays taken of [Baby D] after her death, saw gas in the bloodstream. He was of the view that what he could see was compatible with, consistent with air embolus, but there were other possible explanations. But he did say that he'd not ever come across a baby with this amount of gas in one of the great vessels of the body for which no cause was found.
None of the medical staff on duty that night had been on duty when the [Babies A & B] twins had suffered death and collapse or when [Baby C] collapsed and died.

As for the nursing staff, the only nurse other than Lucy Letby who'd been on duty on any of the previous three cases was Kathryn Percival-Ward, who'd been working the night [Baby B] collapsed, and Elizabeth Marshall, the nursery nurse who'd been on when [Baby C] had collapsed. So two of the other staff had been working one each of the other three incidents.
In the aftermath of [Baby D]'s death there were many messages sent by Lucy Letby to her friends.

[Nurse A], one of the other nurses, had queried what had happened to [Baby D] in the context of what had happened before to [Baby C] and to the [Babies A & B] twins. And Lucy Letby suggested that they were all clearly explicable by natural causes.

When she was interviewed by the police, Lucy Letby accepted that her signature was on some of the documents in [Baby D]'s records in the early hours of 22 June. She said that she didn't remember where she'd been at 1.30 that morning when [Baby D] had first collapsed and said, "I cannot remember how I got involved". But she did confirm that she would have had to use a syringe in the intravenous port to do what she had signed as having done. So she had access to [Baby D]'s bloodstream at the time that we say somebody injected [Baby D] with air.
She seemed to accept in interview that she'd administered medication with a syringe at 5 minutes before the first collapse when [Baby D]'s designated nurse was absent.

In the June 2019 interview she said she couldn't remember calling Caroline Oakley back when [Baby D] had collapsed, Caroline Oakley was the designated nurse, but it was possible that she had. She said she had no recollection of [Baby D] independently of the medical records, and the police were showing her the records when they were interviewing her, just so you understand. She ended that interview by saying that if [Nurse C] said that she, Lucy Letby, was in room 1 alone with [Baby D] at the time of the collapse then she must have been. So she seemed to accept that she was in the room alone at the critical time.

In November 2020 it was put to Lucy Letby that she had searched Facebook for [Baby D]'s parents in the aftermath of [Baby D]'s death. She said that she couldn't remember doing that, but she accepted that she had done and she could not explain why she had done it. Ladies and gentlemen, we suggest that if, as a nurse, you searched for the family of a baby that you had seen die, you would know and remember why you'd done it.
She was asked about messages she'd had with one of her colleagues on 22 June, the day [Baby D] died, in which she described:
"A weird rash looking like overwhelming sepsis."
And she said she couldn't remember having formed that opinion.

She was asked about other messages or another message in which she'd referred to "an element of fate [an element of fate] being involved". She said that it was fate that babies get unwell sometimes, but she would have liked -- sorry, she would have to know the context.
Well, we say that, tragically for [Baby D], her bad luck or fate was the fact that Lucy Letby was working in the neonatal unit that night.

So again, just taking a step back, back from the detail of [Baby D]'s case, [Baby D] is case number 4. So far we have three allegations of injecting small babies with air into their bloodstream and one of injecting air into the stomach. The [Babies A & B] twins, [Baby C] and [Baby D] were all children who deteriorated catastrophically, yet none was expected to have serious problems. Only [Baby B] survived and only Lucy Letby was the constant presence.
We suggest that you'll have to assess all that in the light of — for the reasons we will see we are suggesting that Lucy Letby was the insulin poisoner as well.

blocks.text: [Baby F] is one of the two insulin cases, so important in the overall context. It's an allegation, as you can see, of attempted murder on 5 August, and by reference to count 5, concerning [Baby E], this was the day after [Baby E] had been killed, murdered we say, by Lucy Letby.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Of course, being a twin, [Baby F] was born at about the same time as [Baby E]. He was marginally the younger of the twins. He required some resuscitation at birth.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: He was later put on to a ventilator and given that protein, surfactant, which you'll remember is the thing that's given to premature babies to help with their lungs. You remember us looking at that this morning in the glossary.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: But his initial blood gas readings were within normal range. The breathing tube was taken out on 29 July, so the same day that he was born, at about 10 pm. But he had continuing breathing problems, so the medics re-intubated him. But he was in reasonable shape, his blood sugars were recorded as stable. But then between 3.40 and 6.20 on the morning of 31 July, so 2 days after his birth, he had high blood sugar readings and was prescribed a tiny dose of insulin to help correct it.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: By the time his breathing tube was removed -- sorry, at about that time his breathing tube was removed, but he was given some breathing support, and thereafter he tolerated small amounts of breast milk and he was given fluid nutrients, it's called total parenteral nutrition, TPN for short, also known as Babiven, and that comes out of a bag via a tube into the body, so that was a supplement for his nutrition.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: If it's known in advance, so if the medics have some warning that a particular baby can't take milk for whatever reason and needs to be fed through fluids, then the TPN bag is prepared in the pharmacy unit of the hospital. The system is that a doctor has to write a prescription for TPN, the prescription goes to the pharmacy, the pharmacy prepares the bag and sends the bag back on a daily delivery up to the ward. The bag is individualised, it's a bespoke bag prepared for an individual patient. Okay?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: If for whatever reason the medics don't know that there is going to be a need for total parenteral nutrition to be used for a specific baby, they do have a couple of stock bags on the ward. They're non-specific, they've not been -- nothing's been added to in the pharmacy, or shouldn't have been added to in the pharmacy, and they are kept in reserve.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Just to give you an idea of what we're talking about, I'm going to show you a little representation of what it is we're talking about. This is what a TPN bag looks like. You can see underneath that there are in effect three separate ports. Convention dictates that nothing is added to any of these bags on the ward.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Okay? So it absolutely shouldn't happen. If anything is added to one of these bags, it must be done in the pharmacy in the hospital.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: But despite the fact that that is the convention, one of the ports -- and I think it's the one in the middle of the three -is a port that you can, as a matter of fact, if you wanted to, insert a syringe with a needle. So the needle goes through the port into the bag, and you can inject medicine or whatever into these bags, but it doesn't happen on the wards. If anything has to be added, it has to be added in the pharmacy.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: As a matter of practice in the hospital, insulin is never added to a TPN bag. So not only not added on the wards, because nothing should be added on the wards, but even within the pharmacy the pharmacist would never put insulin in a TPN bag. Because insulin, when it is prescribed for a baby, has to be given via its own infusion and it's usually put into a syringe on a syringe driver which delivers an automatic dose over a period of time.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: One of the primary reasons that insulin is never added to a TPN bag is because of the chemical make-up of insulin and the chemical make-up of the plastic that is used in the bags and in the tubes and in the delivery hardware that actually goes into the baby. Insulin can stick to the plastic or bind to the plastic, so that makes it more difficult to calculate precisely what dose you're giving and that in turn makes it unreliable, which in turn defeats the object of giving insulin in the first place. All right? So insulin never goes into a TPN bag.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: You know from what I told you this morning that on 4 August, [Baby E] had died. Later that morning, on the 4th, the pharmacy unit received a prescription for a TPN bag for [Baby F].
