blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So you've got a drop in blood sugar after bag 1 goes up. New line, new bag. Blood sugar continues to go down. Then there's a third bag coming up at a later stage.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So the point here, ladies and gentlemen, just to make it clear, is that the blood sugar started to drop calamitously while Lucy Letby was there, but continued after she'd gone. So the question is how did that happen?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: It could happen in a number of ways and I'll come to that, but the blood sample that was taken -- a blood sample was taken from [Baby F] at just before 6 o'clock that evening. In other words, about 16 hours or so after that bag was hung, into which we say Lucy Letby put insulin. And that blood sample taken at about 6 o'clock returned a blood glucose level which was very low, very low. So low that if it had remained untreated, it may have caused convulsions, coma, a cessation in breathing, irreversible brain damage and death.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Once that level of blood sugar returned the analysis, which is virtually immediate, a bag of sugar water, dextrose, was put up. So taken off the TPN altogether, put on to dextrose. By 7.30 pm, [Baby F]'s blood sugar levels were virtually normal. So disconnected from the TPN, on to dextrose, within a short period of time virtually normal blood sugar.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: And he had no further episodes of hypoglycaemia at all.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: These events were sufficiently concerning to the medical staff that they ordered a check of what's called his plasma insulin level and the level of another hormone called C-peptide. In most people, if you're not diabetic, your healthy blood glucose levels, your blood sugar levels, are maintained naturally by the body's production of the hormone insulin. You probably all know that already.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: But what you may not know is that when your body produces insulin, it also produces another hormone called C-peptide, and once produced, both insulin and C-peptide break down in the body at similar rates and so the proportion of insulin in your blood is directly proportional to the proportion of C-peptide. The amount of insulin is directly proportionate to the amount of Cpeptide.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: If you're diabetic and you don't produce your own insulin, then your blood glucose levels may be managed by taking synthetic insulin, by injecting insulin, and synthetic insulin or exogenous insulin, insulin coming from outside, doesn't come with C-peptide. Okay? So it follows from that slightly complicated explanation that if your blood is analysed for insulin, the analysis can tell whether your insulin is natural or if it's synthetic or from the outside, exogenous insulin.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So if somebody has an abnormally high insulin level in their blood, together with a very low level of C-peptide, it must be
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: that they have been given or have taken synthetic insulin. Okay? So high insulin with low C-peptide, only conclusion is it's synthetic insulin.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: The blood sample taken from [Baby F] at just before 6 o'clock returned a very high insulin measurement of 4,657 and a very low C-peptide of less than 169. And that, we say, and we don't anticipate that anybody's going to dispute this, at least, means that somebody gave [Baby F] synthetic insulin, somebody poisoned him.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: All experienced medical and nursing members of staff would know the dangers of introducing insulin into any individual whose glucose levels are within the normal range and they would know that hypoglycaemia, low blood sugar, over a prolonged period of time, carries life-threatening risks. No other baby on the neonatal unit at that time was being prescribed insulin.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: [Baby F] therefore couldn't have received the insulin that was intended for somebody else by negligence. And as I have already told you wouldn't have had it put, even if it was a negligent but well-intentioned act, it wouldn't have gone into the TPN bag anyway.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: To give insulin to [Baby F], whoever did it would have had to access the locked fridge on the ward. They would have to use a needle and syringe to remove some insulin from the ampoule in the fridge and either inject it into the TPN bag, that yellow bag that we saw on the screen -- and the stock TPN bags, as a matter of interest, are kept in the same fridge as the insulin.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Or, if they didn't do it that way, they'd have to go to the cot side and inject the insulin directly into the infant, either through a IV line or an intramuscular injection or, and this is what we say happened in this case, inject it into the TPN bag so that it went with the nutrition through the line on a regular basis into the baby.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Both prosecution independent paediatricians concluded that the combination of this grossly elevated insulin level, together with the low C-peptide level and the very low glucose level, was consistent with [Baby F] having received synthetic insulin from the TPN bag, just prior to the discovery of his low blood sugar. It can't have been an accident. And you know who was in the room and you know from the records who hung the bag.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: One of the questions may be whether it went into one bag or two bags, whether it went into the bag that was hung at midnight and whether it also went into the stock bag in the fridge, so if the bag was changed, the stock bag also had insulin in it. We'll see how the evidence emerges on that issue.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: But the fact that this was synthetic insulin, the prosecution say, is conclusively proved by the evidence of a doctor called Professor Peter Hindmarsh.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Summarising what Professor Hindmarsh says, he identifies first of all this disparity between the high level of insulin and the low level of C-peptide and says, well, that means that this must be a case of synthetic insulin. But Professor Hindmarsh takes it a bit further because he says it has to have gone in through the TPN bag rather than through the other possibilities because the low blood sugar, the hypoglycaemia, went on for such a long period of time and it went on for such a long period of time despite the fact that [Baby F] was given five separate injections of 10% dextrose and he was on a dextrose or glucose bag as well to up his blood sugar.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Professor Hindmarsh put his mind to the issue of how it could be that if the original bag had been changed, how could it be that the problem, the hypoglycaemia continued, despite the fact that the original bag had been changed. He comes up with a number of possibilities. The first is that the original bag wasn't replaced, it was simply carried on. The second is that the stock bag in the fridge, which happens to be where the insulin is kept, had already been contaminated with insulin. And the third possibility is that some part of the giving set, which is the bit that goes into the patient, was contaminated by insulin from the first bag and that insulin had bound to the plastic in the giving set and therefore continued to leech out of the plastic, even though the bag was changed and the second bag didn't have insulin in it. So it's all a bit of a headache, but it's this point about the binding of insulin to plastic that introduces the third possibility.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: But the bottom line, ladies and gentlemen, we say, is that there can be no doubt that somebody contaminated that original bag with insulin and that because of that, and because of the possibility that the stock bag was contaminated as well, the problem continued through the day.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: This case, [Baby F]'s case, will have to be considered, and I will consider it, tomorrow in conjunction with [Baby L]'s case, because [Baby L], you will remember from what I told you yesterday, is the other baby who was poisoned with insulin and you'll remember that only two people that were on the [Baby F] shift were on the [Baby L] shift and one of them is sitting in the dock. Okay?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So moving on to the interviews, Lucy Letby was, in July 2018, asked about this particular night shift of 4 into 5 August. She confirmed that she remembered [Baby F]. She said she had no
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: recollection of the incident other than looking at the notes there. She said she'd not been [Baby F]'s designated nurse and had not been involved in his care other than as shown by the notes.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: She was asked about that chart that I have just shown you, showing the TPN bags. She said that TPN was kept in a locked fridge next to the nurses' station in the equipment room. She said that the insulin was kept in the same fridge. She confirmed that her signature was on the TPN form with [Nurse A] and that's what we've just seen. She said she had no independent recollection of having had any involvement with administering the contents of the TPN bag to [Baby F].
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: She confirmed that she had given [Baby F] glucose boluses, so injections of glucose, at 3.50, 4.10 and 4.20, so even though she wasn't his designated nurse she was giving him the glucose boluses following the discovery of his hypoglycaemia.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: She confirmed that at 5 o'clock that morning on that shift she'd taken observations of [Baby F] and was "hands on with him" at that time. She suggested that she must have been doing all that for someone who was on a break. She said that the blood sugar reading that she'd taken at 5 am was "a little bit low", to use her phrase, and she confirmed that it was her signature on the fluid charts for [Baby F] at 3.50, 4.10 and 4.20, all of which reflected treatments for low blood sugar.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: And later in the interview, she confirmed that she'd signed for a lipid syringe. Do you remember the syringe that sometimes goes with the liquid feed, the TPN, for a baby that isn't getting milk? That lipid syringe had been given to [Baby F] the shift before, at 01.10 in the morning on 3 August.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: I just want to show you that, please. Again with my highlighting. You see at the bottom -- well, let's go down. It's prepared on 31 July, at the top, for use on 2 August. Here you can see on the next highlighted bit:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "For administration up to 48 hours commencing 23.30 hours on the 2nd."
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's the manual correction that I was talking about that is replicated on the TPN bag as well.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: The hole in the page which has been photocopied should say "lipid" there:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "Lipid feed volume: 15 millilitres per kilo, supplied in a separate syringe."
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: And you can see at the bottom in handwriting "lipid" and then a number, "3/8/15, 0010", and that's Lucy Letby's signature. She should have got somebody else to co-sign that and she didn't.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: She accepted that that signature tended to suggest that she had administered it. Interestingly, at the end of that interview, this is the 2018 interview, she asked the police whether they had access to the TPN bag that she had connected. So the TPN bag that we say someone, she, had put insulin into, she was asking the police in the interview, "Have you got the bag?"
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: In the June 2019 interview, she said that the order of signatures on charts, you see the double signatures, didn't necessarily identify who had administered the treatment and who was co-signing for a treatment. And she agreed that the idea that insulin had been administered accidentally could be excluded because all the nursing and medical staff knew the dangers and the idea it was happening by mistake is just not feasible.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: In November 2020 she was asked why she had searched on social media for [parents of Babies E & F]. Remember me telling you about this just before we broke for lunch?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: She said she didn't remember doing it and thought it might be to see how [Baby F] was doing.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: She was asked some texts she had sent or a text she sent to a colleague about [Baby F]'s blood sugar levels and that had been at 8 o'clock after her shift and said, "Well, I must have looked on his chart".
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Ladies and gentlemen, I'm just taking a step back again. Once again a case involving a child for whom Lucy Letby was not the designated nurse, but in whom she clearly took a close interest. We say for reasons that are self-evident on the facts of this individual case, but for reasons that I'll expand on when we get to [Baby L], that there's no doubt that this is a case of insulin poisoning and that whoever did it used a method which would never be used legitimately in a hospital setting.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: The fact that it was done through the TPN bag tells you that it wasn't a genuine mistake, doesn't it, and that whoever did it was trying to avoid detection? Only a few people had the opportunity and, as I've said before, taken together with what was later to happen to [Baby L], we suggest that there is really only one credible candidate for the poisoner: the same person who was present at all the unexpected collapses and deaths at the Countess of Chester neonatal unit.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So that's the case of [Baby F].
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Can we move on to [Baby G], the seventh child. If we go back to the indictment, please, ladies and gentlemen. Page 3, please. You can see there are three counts: count 7, attempted murder on 7 September; count 8, attempted murder on 21 September at about 10.15 in the morning; and then count 9, also on 21 September at about 15.30 hours, attempted murder again. So we say Lucy Letby tried to kill [Baby G] on three occasions and occasions 2 and 3 were on the same shift.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: [Baby G] was born on 31 May 2015, so as a matter of fact, even though she comes in midway through the chronology of the counts, she was the first born of all the children in this case.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: She was born on 31 May at Arrowe Park Hospital.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Arrowe Park Hospital is on the Wirral and it is what the medics refer to as a tertiary centre. In the Merseyside/Cheshire area, which is the geographical area that we're dealing with in this case, the tertiary centres that you're going to hear about are Arrowe Park Hospital and the Liverpool Women's Hospital.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: In very general terms, the tertiary centres deal with the most difficult cases. Okay? So they're the level 3 centres. The Countess of Chester was a level 2.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Below level 2 is level 1.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: [Baby G] was born at a gestational age of 23 weeks and 6 days, so exceptionally premature given that the "standard" pregnancy is 40 weeks. Twenty-three weeks and 6 days, so at the margins of survivability.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: [Baby G]'s parents are [Parents of Baby G], and when she was born [Baby G] weighed 535 grams, 1 pound and 2 ounces. Tiny. [Baby G] spent the early part of her life at Arrowe Park Hospital and she suffered various problems, including bleeding on her lungs on 29 June.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Her initial life was typical of a baby born at such an early stage. She had a number of septic or suspected septic episodes requiring antibiotics. She received nine blood transfusions, she had multiple X-rays of her chest and abdomen and underwent heart scans. She also received several brain ultrasound scans, which importantly were all reported as normal.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: On 13 August, so in round terms 10 or 11 weeks after her birth, when she would have been at a gestational age of 34 weeks and 3 days, she was transferred from the tertiary centre at Arrowe Park to the Countess of Chester neonatal unit. And she was clinically stable for the first couple of weeks following her
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: transfer to Chester and she was being fed expressed breast milk; so she was doing well.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So event 1, which is count 7. The night shift of 6 to 7 September 2015, so 3 weeks or so after she'd come from Arrowe Park to Chester. That night, [Nurse E] was the designated nurse for [Baby G] and [Baby G] was in nursery 2. There were seven babies in the unit that night and five nursing staff.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: The consultant was Stephen Brearey, the registrar Alison Ventress, the SHO Charlotte Newton and the nurses on duty were Ailsa Simpson, Christopher Booth, [Nurse E] and Lucy Letby. The nursery nurse was Lisa Walker.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Lucy Letby's baby that night I'll refer to by the initials IH. IH was in nursery 1. It was a significant date, ladies and gentlemen, because 100 days had passed since [Baby G] had been born. The nurses mark these sorts of anniversaries, or milestones would be a better word, by putting up a banner and making a cake.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: The feeding charts show that [Baby G] was taking bottles of 45 millilitres of milk, which, when you've heard of some of these babies being fed half a millilitre, sounds like a gargantuan amount, doesn't it?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Forty-five millilitres of milk, 100 days old, and she took that from a bottle. She took that from a bottle at 11 o'clock, 11 pm, on 6 September. [Baby G] was being fed every 3 hours, alternately by bottle and then NGT, so down the tube.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: At 2 o'clock in the morning on 7 September, [Nurse E] aspirated the NGT tube, so she drew up to see if there was anything in [Baby G]'s stomach, she checked that there was no residual milk, she checked the positioning of the tube and then she fed a sleeping [Baby G] 45 millilitres of milk through the tube. So it was alternate -- bottle, tube, bottle, tube -- and this was tube.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: When she had drawn up the aspirate, she found minimal aspirates of a quantity that was not sufficient to prevent feeding and meant, importantly, that before she was fed [Baby G]'s stomach had been empty, pretty much empty. So zero or pretty much zero plus 45 millilitres went down. Then [Nurse E] took her scheduled 1-hour break.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: And the system was on the night shifts that all the nurses were entitled to an hour's break at some time in the shift. The way it would work would be that they would ask one of their colleagues to keep an eye on their baby while they took their break.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: There's nothing recorded in the notes as to who was asked to keep an eye on [Baby G]. So [Baby G] had been fed at 2 o'clock. [Nurse E] went on her break. And at 2.15, the shift leader, Ailsa Simpson says that she was sitting with Lucy Letby at the nursing station when she heard [Baby G] vomiting, followed by the sound of [Baby G]'s alarm. Ailsa Simpson remembers jumping up and running into the nursery with Lucy Letby, and at a later stage, Ailsa Simpson marked a photograph with the location of the vomit. I just want to show you this photograph.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So [Baby G] was in a cot in that position, that type of a cot, 100 days old but still only 34.5 weeks gestation.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: The vomit that [Baby G] produced landed in the areas marked with the black circles.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: (Photograph shown to the court)

Now, Ailsa Simpson's memory of being sitting at the nursing station in the time before [Baby G] produced that vomit, we suggest, cannot be accurate because entries in some of the other children's medical records show that it just can't be right because she and Lucy Letby are making entries in the time that she recalls that she was sitting with Lucy Letby.

But be that as it may, [Baby G], when she produced the vomit, which is denoted by those three black circles, suffered a collapse and when Ailsa Simpson and Lucy Letby went in, she wasn't breathing. The registrar, Dr Ventress, was called urgently at 2.35, and Dr Ventress observed that [Baby G] appeared uncomfortable and her abdomen appeared purple and distended, so swollen. Her blood oxygen levels, her sats, had fallen to 80%, and she had suffered what were recorded as two projectile vomits.

And despite the fact that before she had been fed by [Nurse E], there'd been nothing or virtually nothing in [Baby G]'s stomach. When the doctor came they aspirated [Baby G]'s stomach. In other words they took out what remained in [Baby G]'s stomach, and what they took out was 45 millilitres of milk. You've got the point I'm sure: zero plus 45 equals 45. The vomit that goes in the cot on the floor and on the chair generated with a force -imagine a tiny 34-week gestation baby producing the force to vomit on the chair next to the -- from lying in the cot, out of the cot on to the floor and on to the chair. You aspirate the contents of the baby's stomach and you find 45 millilitres of feed, but only 45 went in.
So how do we account for what came out with sufficient force to go in the cot, on the floor and on the chair? Not only was lots
of -- 45 millilitres of milk taken out of [Baby G]'s stomach, but lots of air came out as well.

Prior to being fed by [Nurse E] at 2 o'clock, [Baby G] had been perfectly well. The X-rays that were taken after this episode show the air that was in her abdomen and her intestines, the stuff that hadn't been drawn out by aspirating the NGT, and also show -- she had to be intubated, show that that was correctly positioned.

Perhaps unsurprisingly, that night, [Baby G] suffered further deteriorations, leading to the fact that she had to be intubated and ventilated. And as she was being ventilated, as Dr Ventress looked down [Baby G]'s throat, the ventilator, she saw some bloodstained fluid.
[Baby C], [Baby E] and now [Baby G].

At 5.30 that morning, [Baby G] desaturated despite being ventilated, and so the tube and the ventilator were changed as a precaution. At 6.05 she had a further desaturation and 100 millilitres of air were aspirated from her NG tube. When the breathing tube was removed, the registrar noted there were thick secretions in her mouth and a blood clot at the end of the breathing tube.
And thereafter, [Baby G] demonstrated signs of infection.

[Baby G] was sent back to the tertiary centre at Arrowe Park in the early hours of 8 September and she made a remarkable recovery. She was then sent back to Chester on the 16th. This pattern of a child suffering a life-threatening collapse, being transferred out of Chester, going somewhere else and making a remarkable recovery is something that we are going to see repeated in some of the cases that I have yet got to explain to you.

Before I get to the mechanism of what we're suggesting, although I'm sure you've probably worked it out already from 45 coming out and 45 going in, but having the vomit and lots of air, I'm sure you've worked out what we're saying about the first one.
But before I get to the explanation I'm going to explain to you the two incidents that happened on 21 September.

The second incident, and this is the one that's particularised or alleged in count 8, so the timing is about 10.15 in the morning. This was 21 September, which is about 5 days after [Baby G]'s return from Arrowe Park. And [Baby G] was so well by this stage that she was due to have her immunisations. As most
parents probably know, you don't give immunisations to a child who isn't well. So she was that well.

At 6 that morning, she was given a 45-millilitre bottle of milk. And then there was a handover of staff from about 7.30. The team that came on at 8 o'clock was the day shift and this is the first of the day shifts that we will consider. The nurses on the day shift were Caroline Bennion, Lucy Letby, [Nurse B], Shelley Tomlins, Caroline Oakley, together with a selection of other doctors and managers. And Lucy Letby was [Baby G]'s designated nurse, as she was to the other two children who were in room 4 with [Baby G]. So by this stage [Baby G] has reached the end of the process in the neonatal unit in the sense of the furthest room from the intensive care unit.

That morning, [Baby G] was fed at 9.15 with a 40-millilitre feed of milk via the NG tube by Lucy Letby and within an hour and 5 minutes she projectile vomited twice. She was apnoeic, which means she wasn't breathing, and she suffered a brief selfresolving colour loss and her blood saturations fell to a lifethreatening 30%.
So [Baby G] had the same problem that she had on 7 September, this time following a documented feed from Lucy Letby. [Baby G], who had recovered, gone back, has the same problem.

[Baby G] was well when she was seen by the doctor at 10.30, although her heart rate had increased and her temperature was low. And the nurses thought that her abdomen was more distended, more swollen than usual.

At 11.30, [Nurse B] took over [Baby G]'s care from Lucy Letby because Lucy Letby had the other two children in room 4. [Nurse B] undertook all the necessary observations and noted that [Baby G] was connected to what's called a Masimo monitor, which is a portable device attached to the patient by a sensor that continually measures oxygen saturations and heart rate levels and we've got a picture of one of these for you.
(Photograph shown to the court)
You can see the readings are set out on the screen.
There are videos which we're going to show you as part of the evidence right at the beginning so you're familiar with what all these bits of equipment look like.
These monitors should remain on and attached constantly to the baby and, of course, it probably goes out saying, I'm sure, can't be turned off by the baby.

At about 15.30 that afternoon, so we're moving on to count 9, ladies and gentlemen, Dr Gibbs, who was the consultant, was called to cannulate [Baby G], to put a line into [Baby G]. [Baby G]'s mum left the nursery whilst that was done, privacy screens were put round [Baby G]'s cot, [Baby G] was put on to a trolley, still attached to her Masimo monitor, and [Nurse B] attended to other duties whilst Dr Gibbs undertook the necessary procedure. As a matter of fact, [Nurse B] had another baby in room number 1.

Dr Gibbs, when he was asked about this, couldn't remember whether the Masimo monitor was switched off whilst he was fitting the cannula. But what he says is that it is his normal practice to transfer the sensor from one limb to another whilst he's doing a procedure or, if it is necessary to detach the monitor, he puts it back on as soon as possible. You may think that's common sense.
Dr Gibbs also says that having conducted this procedure, if [Baby G] hadn't been completely stable, he wouldn't have left her and again that's common sense, isn't it?

Well, after Dr Gibbs had gone, but [Baby G] was still behind the screen, [Nurse B] responded to Lucy Letby's shout for help. And when [Nurse B] attended she noticed that [Baby G]'s monitor had been switched off, the power was off. [Baby G] was dusky and struggling to breathe and Lucy Letby was giving her ventilation breaths.
Mercifully, [Baby G] responded to the treatment.
In a text sent that evening to [Nurse A], Lucy Letby said:
"[[Baby G]] looked rubbish when I took over this morning, then she vomited at 9 and I got her screened. Mum says she hasn't been herself for a couple of days."
But as I have told you, she was due to have her immunisations and we suggest that wouldn't have been contemplated if [Baby G] had not been in good condition.
There had been no significant issues with [Baby G] at all that shift until Lucy Letby got involved. [Baby G] vomited in the first part of the shift because somebody gave her excessive milk and air.

An MRI scan of [Baby G]'s brain between the first incident at the beginning of September and the second two incidents at the end of September revealed -- sorry, no, no, I'm getting confused. Sorry, I am right.

An MRI scan taken between the first incident, in other words between count 7 and between counts 8 and 9, revealed that [Baby G] had suffered brain damage. So what had happened to her in the Countess of Chester on 7 September, that projectile vomiting out of the cot on to the floor and on to the chair, had resulted in irreversible brain damage. And that was confirmed in a later scan as well.

Well, dealing with those incidents individually, starting with 7 September, both Dr Evans and Dr Bohin concluded what you have probably worked out for yourselves already, that [Baby G], when she vomited on to the chair, had received excessive milk and probably air through her NG tube at about 2 o'clock, which you'll remember is the time that [Nurse E] had fed her and gone off.

The reasoning is common sense. It's the inconsistency between the amount that she was fed and the amount that was aspirated when you add in what she vomited. Putting it simply, the milk in the vomit didn't come from nowhere, did it, and can only be accounted for by somebody feeding an excessive quantity to [Baby G]?

That doesn't happen by accident. There are parallels, aren't there, ladies and gentlemen, with what I've already told you about [Baby C]? And you are going to hear further parallels in the cases of [Baby I], [Baby P] and [Baby Q].

[Baby G]'s first deterioration on 21 September showed a similar pattern to what had happened on the 7th, didn't it? [Baby G] suffered another potentially life-threatening episode of vomiting and desaturation and produced projectile vomits.

On the second occasion, count 9, in the afternoon, when she was behind a screen, somebody switched off the monitor when [Baby G] collapsed. Dr Gibbs didn't. [Baby G] didn't do it. And she was discovered by Lucy Letby.
There is a common theme running through all these cases, isn't there?
My Lord, I'm going to go on -- sorry, I'll deal with the interviews.
Just to tell you what Lucy Letby said when she was interviewed, so we're going back to the 7th, first of all, [Nurse E] feeding, going on the break, and the projectile vomit.
Lucy Letby said that she remembered that [Nurse E] had been on her break when the incident had happened with [Baby G] in nursery 2 on 7 September.

She, Lucy Letby, couldn't remember who she had been assigned to care for, she said that the notes of [Baby G] suggested that she had taken over her care at 2 o'clock that morning but she couldn't remember why that was and we say the reason is because [Nurse E] said, "Can you look after her while I go on my break?"

She said she did remember [Baby G] vomiting but she couldn't remember what had happened in the 15 minutes before the vomit, and she was asked about how it could be that [Baby G] was full of air if, before [Nurse E] had fed her 45mls, she'd aspirated the NG tube and there'd been nothing significant, how could it be that after the vomit [Baby G] was full of air? And Lucy Letby suggested that the air must have come about as a result of the vomiting or because [Baby G] had some sort of infection. So if the evidence about the aspiration is right, this is air that produced itself within -- or arrived within 15 minutes or so.

She said that she had been the person that had withdrawn the 45 millilitres of milk after that episode and that air had come with it. She said that she had seen [Baby G] vomiting and didn't remember why she'd gone in when she'd seen [Baby G] vomiting, but then that it was possible that it was a result of hearing her vomit that she'd gone in. She said that she'd noticed discolouration on [Baby G]'s abdomen at the time she was vomiting but couldn't now, in the context of the interview, describe it because she couldn't really recall it very clearly. Neither could she recall whether she'd been there when [Baby G] had desaturated later in the shift.
She was asked about events with [Baby G] on 21 September and she confirmed her writing on the documents.

She said she vaguely remembered the day: [Baby G] had been in nursery 4 where she'd looked after her for a period in the morning and she accepted that at the beginning of the shift she had been [Baby G]'s designated nurse, though she had no recollection, she said, of [Baby G] vomiting at 10.15. So count 8.
Later in the interview, the first incident was revisited and she was asked about the content of a witness statement that had been made by [Nurse E].

Lucy Letby accepted that because the amount of milk aspirated after the vomit had been equal to what [Baby G] had been fed, there were really only two alternatives: either [Baby G] had been given far more than she should have been or she had not digested her earlier feed. She accepted that it was standard practice to aspirate the NG tube before feeding to check of the tube was correctly placed and that the previous feed had been
digested, and if that had been done and milk had come back, in other words if [Baby G] had had milk before she was fed, she would "not necessarily" have been fed at all.

And she accepted, Lucy Letby did, that the clear inference to be drawn was that [Baby G] had been given excessive milk and air via the NG tube. She denied responsibility for either of those eventualities.

With regard to the first incident on 21 September she said that the notes showed that she had aspirated 30mls of milk from [Baby G]'s stomach just before 9 o'clock but then fed [Baby G] 40mls, then had aspirated and discarded 30mls of milk from [Baby G] at 10.15, after she'd vomited. And it was suggested by the police that if there had been two milky vomits before the aspiration at 10.15 that too showed that [Baby G] must have been fed much more than had been recorded.

So two events, we say, where the records suggest [Baby G] must have received much more than she should have done. And again, Lucy Letby denied either overfeeding or injecting air into [Baby G]'s stomach via a nasogastric tube.
In November 2020 she was asked about the second of the incidents on 21 September, the incident where the monitor, the Masimo monitor, was switched off. She denied having switched it off.

She was then asked about Facebook searches that she'd done on [Baby G]'s parents, including one that she'd done on 21 September, the very same day as the final two attempts, we say, to kill [Baby G]. She had said she had no recollection of having searched for [Baby G]'s parents.

We suggest that she knows very well why she did it and you can dismiss the idea that she had forgotten why she did it when she was interviewed. And the fact that she wasn't prepared to explain why she did it speaks volumes.

A remarkable feature of the interest that Lucy Letby showed in [Mother of Baby G], who is [Baby G]'s mum, was that within a minute or two of looking for [Mother of Baby G] on Facebook on 5 November, she also searched for [Mother of Babies E & F] -- do you remember the lady that saw blood round the mouth of [Baby E]? And also searched for a lady called [Mother of Baby I]. [Mother of Babies E & F], the lady that interrupted her attack on [Mother of Babies E & F]'s son.
[Mother of Baby I], a case that I have yet to explain to you.
When we get to [Mother of Baby I]'s case, though -- sorry, [Baby I]'s case, you will see some similarities with [Baby G]'s case.
Repeated attacks by Lucy Letby, which sadly, tragically, in [Baby I]’s case, resulted in her death. And [Baby I] too was to be injected with air.

So again, ladies and gentlemen, just taking a step back from the detail, we say that the facts really speak for themselves in [Baby G]'s case. The practice, the invariable practice -- and you will see it noted in the paperwork -- was that the nurses, before feeding a child, would check that the child's stomach was empty.

That was done in [Baby G]'s case and nothing came up, which means there was nothing in her stomach. She was fed, the designated nurse went on a break, and 15 minutes later [Baby G] produced projectile vomits of such force that they left the cot and landed on a nearby chair and the floor. [Baby G] collapsed and stopped breathing and the amount of milk taken out equalled the amount that supposedly had gone in and the amount that was taken out also included lots of air. A similar episode a few weeks later, and as a result, [Baby G] has been left severely disabled.
On the second occasion, the second incident, somebody detached the monitor from [Baby G], who was behind a screen, and was discovered by Lucy Letby.

Ladies and gentlemen, these were not naturally occurring or random events, they were deliberate attempts to kill using slightly different methods by which Lucy Letby sought to give the appearance of chance events at the neonatal unit in the Countess of Chester Hospital.
My Lord, it may be that that's a good place.
It certainly is, thank you very much, Mr Johnson. It's almost 3.45.
